title: A leg ulcer sent for compression, and an ABI that looks too good
objective: Use toe-brachial index and pedal Doppler waveforms with the ABI when vessels may be calcified, and treat ankle pressure below 50 mm Hg or ABI below 0.5 as a sign of poor healing and higher amputation risk
secondaryObjectives: Use high compression to knee height as the core venous ulcer treatment, drop to 20 mm Hg or less while waiting for vascular testing, and avoid it with arterial occlusion, ABPI under 0.5, heart failure or thrombosis

Measure the ankle-brachial index correctly: use the highest ankle systolic pressure over the higher brachial pressure, measuring both arms, and suspect falsely high values in calcified vessels (diabetes, CKD, old age)

Recognize arterial disease: claudication relieved by rest, then ischemic forefoot rest pain when the legs are raised that eases with the foot dependent; arterial ulcers are deep, dry and sit on toes, dorsum or anterior leg

brief.situation: 10:00 in an outpatient wound clinic. You are the physical therapist. Mr. Delgado, 71, is referred by his primary care physician: 'Venous leg ulcer, right lateral ankle, 6 weeks, not healing. Please start multilayer compression.'
handover: Type 2 diabetes for 22 years, chronic kidney disease stage 3, former smoker. Ankle swelling by evening.
Ulcer dressed at home by his daughter with gauze.
Clinic equipment: handheld Doppler, ankle and toe cuffs with a photoplethysmography sensor, multilayer compression kits.
Clinic policy: the vascular surgery service takes same-day calls for limb-threatening ischemia.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Each measurement takes the time on its button. Decide what to measure, what the numbers mean and what to do.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Is this a venous ulcer that needs compression? What do the vascular numbers mean, and what do you do?

parts.label: Interpretation
parts.criteria: An ABI of 1.48 with arteries the cuff cannot compress is falsely high (diabetes, kidney disease); toe pressure 24 mmHg and TBI 0.17 with monophasic pedal waveforms, absent pulses and rest pain that eases dependent show severe arterial disease; the ulcer looks arterial.
parts.modelAnswer: The ABI of 1.48 is not reassuring: his arteries are calcified and would not compress. His toe pressure is 24 with a TBI of 0.17, the pedal signals are monophasic, the pulses are absent and he has rest pain relieved by hanging the foot down. This is severe arterial disease, not a venous ulcer.

parts.label: Action
parts.criteria: No compression of any strength; dry protective dressing and offloading; same-day call to vascular surgery for urgent assessment; tells the referring physician.
parts.modelAnswer: No compression. Dress and protect the ulcer and call vascular surgery today for an urgent assessment, because a toe pressure under 30 is a threshold for urgent consultation. Then tell his physician why I did not start compression.

expertPath.text: History: claudication, and rest pain at night eased by hanging the foot down. Look at the ulcer: punched-out, pale, dry, over the lateral malleolus.
ABI 1.48 with an artery the cuff cannot compress: falsely high. Do not stop there.
Pedal Doppler: monophasic. Toe pressure 24 mmHg, TBI 0.17. Severe ischemia: no compression.
Dress and offload. Call vascular surgery for an urgent assessment today; tell his physician.

injury.headline: An ischemic injury under the wrap
injury.body: Compression on a limb with severe arterial disease cuts off what flow is left. With an unreliable ABI, check toe pressure and waveforms before any compression.

urgentVascular.headline: Severe ischemia found; urgent vascular care
urgentVascular.body: You did not trust an ABI above 1.3, measured toe pressure and pedal waveforms, kept compression off and called vascular surgery the same visit. That is the expert path.

referredGaps.headline: Referred, with gaps
referredGaps.body: Check whether you measured beyond the ABI, whether any compression went on, and whether the referral matched the urgency of a toe pressure under 30 mmHg.

time_up.headline: No plan
time_up.body: A referral diagnosis is a hypothesis. Test it, then act on what the limb shows.

scoring.modelReasoning: In a long-standing diabetic with kidney disease, an ABI of 1.48 with an artery the cuff cannot compress is falsely high and says nothing about perfusion. Toe pressure and the toe-brachial index, with pedal Doppler waveforms, are the measures that still work: here a toe pressure of 24 mmHg, a TBI of 0.17 and monophasic signals, with absent pulses, rest pain eased by dependency and a pale punched-out ulcer, mean severe arterial disease. A toe pressure under 30 mmHg calls for urgent vascular consultation, and compression of any strength is unsafe on a limb this ischemic, so no compression, protect and offload the ulcer, call vascular surgery today and correct the referral.
